name: Olga Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pack orders at a mail-order garden and pet supplies company just outside our market town. Seeds, bird feeders, bags of compost, dog beds, all sent out to people's doors. I pick from the racks, pack into boxes with paper filling, and label them. Spring is mad busy, winter is very quiet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a family firm, the owner still walks round at Christmas with chocolates. And I like the gardening customers, they write little notes asking us to pack the seedlings gently. What wears me out is lifting the forty-litre compost bags, and the winter when they cut us to three days. My team leader, Bev, says I'm careful but slow, which I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we can all get on with our lives. I'd say it at work and at church coffee after the service. I don't really post opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me the worries are the old ones. Every winter my hours drop to three days a week, and every winter I tell myself next year we'll have a baby. Marco, my husband, is a plumber's mate, so his money isn't huge either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and ask Bev about covering more shifts in winter, like stock counts. We have about three months of bills saved, and I'd try to build that to five before we try for a baby. I'd keep my spending small, no new phone this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but a bit stuck. Same worries, just without the AI ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a winter on three days look like for your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We cover it, but only just, and nothing goes into savings from November to February. Marco does extra call-outs with his boss in the cold snaps, burst pipes, so that helps. We eat a lot of soup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI now and then. For what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly recipes, and once to help write the church newsletter. My friend Jo at choir showed me. I'm not against it, I just don't need it much.

say: I'd say we can all **get on** with our lives.
I'd say it at work and at **church coffee**, not online.
think: The real worry is **winter hours** dropping to three days.
Each year we **put off a baby** because money is tight.
do: Ask Bev for **winter stock count** shifts.
Build savings from three to **five months** before trying for a baby.
feel: **Steady** but a bit **stuck** with the same old worries.

fieldNote: **Seasonal hours** and family plans are her main pressures.
Her husband Marco's **plumber's mate** wage is modest too.
She uses AI lightly, for **recipes and newsletters**.

steps.text: Ask Bev for winter stock count shifts
Build savings to five months before trying for a baby
Skip the new phone this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office girls answering emails might need to worry, but packing is still packing. I'd say it at work. I'd probably also say that firms should train their own people rather than lay them off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our customer service is three women answering emails about late seeds, and that's exactly what the AI would take. The packing would change slower. A family firm that still prints its catalogue on paper is not going to buy a robot next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep packing and maybe ask to learn the new AI system if they bring one in for the orders, so I'm useful. I'd keep saving. Marco and I would still try for a baby next year if things stayed like this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, mostly for the customer service ladies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: June in customer service. She's sixty and she knows every gardening question by heart. If a computer answers the emails, I don't know where she'd go at her age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the firm got sold to a bigger company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would change everything. Big companies love robots. I'd start looking at something else then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast and nobody asked us. I'd say families and churches will have to look after each other. At work I'd tell people not to panic, even though I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI by 2028 means our office is just a computer. By 2031 robots can pack seeds and compost, and even a small firm would buy them when they're cheap. If robots are packing seeds by 2031, I'd want our first baby before then, while my husband and I both still have wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try for a baby straight away instead of waiting. I'd look into a horticulture apprenticeship at the big plant nursery near us, because growing things is hands-on and varied. I'd cut back on everything else to build the savings to six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like the floor's tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a baby a big step when work might go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and Marco would say the same. But if we wait for a safe time, we might never have one. My mother had me when my dad was out of work, and we were fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An apprenticeship that pays, so I can learn without losing money. And our church, people there help each other with meals and childcare.

I'd say **families and churches** must look after each other.
think: Robots packing **by 2031** would reach even a small firm once cheap.
I'd want our **first baby** while we both still earn.
do: Try for a **baby straight away** instead of waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, so firms should start training people now. I'd say it at work and at church. I'd vote for whoever backs apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Packing goes by about 2034, the office by 2031. That gives me time to have a baby and still retrain. I'd rather learn to grow the plants than keep packing the seeds, because growing still needs a person in the mud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd look into the nursery apprenticeship and maybe start part-time when it opens. I'd keep saving and keep working. Marco and I would try for a baby in the second year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel I had a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you balance a baby and an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother would help, she's only two streets away. And the nursery takes part-timers in autumn and winter. It would be hard, but people manage harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to help with any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe to find the right courses, Jo at choir could show me. I'd try it once someone I trust had used it for the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far enough away that we can plan sensibly. People shouldn't panic. I'd say that at work and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough for my husband Marco to get his plumbing ticket, and plumbers will be needed long after packers. That takes pressure off me. I'd still want something better than packing by 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have our baby in the next year or two, keep packing, and encourage Marco to do his plumbing qualification. Once the baby's at nursery, I'd look at the horticulture course. Keep saving steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, with something to keep an eye on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you hurry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm got sold or put a robot on trial. Then I'd start the course sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change how you'd raise your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn something with their hands and something with their heads. And to go to church, to have people around them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because we'd be trying to start a family just as everything changes. What would help is paid apprenticeships for adults and our church community pulling together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. Faith, family and a bit of savings got my grandparents through worse than robots. I think it would get us through too.

headlineQuote: Faith, family and a bit of savings got my grandparents through worse than robots.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old packer** at a family-run garden and pet supplies firm, careful but slow.
She and her husband Marco want a **first baby**, held back by winter hours and modest wages.
She is **traditional**, backs apprenticeships, and leans on church and family.
Faster AGI makes her want the baby **sooner**, and she eyes a **horticulture** apprenticeship.
Her mood is **uneasy** in slow scenarios and **alarmed** by AGI in 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, arriving just as they try to start a family.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for adults and a church community that pulls together.
